sweep_summary: Shilluk (shil1265, in catalog as set by morphology on Westermann 1912 'accent on the stem-syllable'). Of the 22 title hits only two concern Shilluk stress: Reid 2009 (held by the project, read: p. 27 sets stress aside, Gilley's stressed/unstressed words reanalysed as vowel length or High Fall -- silent on stem-vs-affix prominence) and Gilley 2003 'The feature of stress in Nilotic' (FAB 15, pp. 99-120; not open, publisher PDF EUR 39.80; its key passage on p. 104 is quoted verbatim in Remijsen, Ayoker & Jorgensen 2019, held by the project: stress = binary paradigmatic feature on the stem syllable realised as vowel shortening, not a positional rule -- refines the record; priority high). Le Clezio 1995 is an L2-English chapter (Routledge TOC. paywalled, low priority). Bogers et al. 1986 has no Shilluk chapter (Crossref TOC saved). The remaining 18 items are general works, other languages (Athabaskan, Mayo, SE Asia, Lango, Guyanese, AAE) or L2 studies -- none relevant. 10 p. 8 (stress not on initial/final affix vowel; most words monosyllabic), which confirms but does not supersede the deciding source. no reclassification indicated; Gilley 1992 (SIL PL 103, print only) and Gilley 2003 remain the unread works that could settle whether Shilluk has word stress at all.archive. DuckDuckGo/the Internet Archive/UChicago could not be reached by automated download.

new_statements.quote: 10. The Accentuation, that is the emphasis laid on a syllable or a word, is not of such importance as it is in European languages, chiefly for the simple reason that most of the words are monosyllabic. Note the following rule: the stress does not lie on the vowel beginning or ending a word, except where the last vowel is an independent element, as: a bind "I came", here the final "a" means "I"; in this case the ending vowel has its own accent.
new_statements.citation: Westermann, Diedrich. 1912. A short grammar of the Shilluk language. Philadelphia: Board of Foreign Missions of the United Presbyterian Church of N.A. / Berlin: Dietrich Reimer. Sec. 10 'The Accentuation', p. 8.
new_statements.locator: sec. 10, p. 8 (djvu the text layer); cf. sec. 8 'The Intonation', p. 7 (lines 529-540)
new_statements.reading: Same observer and year as the catalog's deciding source (Westermann 1912, The Shilluk People, pp. 21-23). Word stress is marginal because most words are monosyllabic; in polysyllables the stress does not fall on an initial or final (affixal) vowel unless that vowel is an independent morpheme -- i.e. stress sits on the stem, which is what the catalog codes as set by morphology. It is consistent with, but no stronger than, the deciding quote, and Westermann himself flags accent as of little importance. Nothing in the 22 works with stress in the title yields a first-hand modern positional-stress statement; the modern literature (Reid 2009, read; Gilley 2003 via Remijsen et al. 2019's verbatim quotation) treats 'stress' only as Gilley's paradigmatic stem-syllable feature, since reanalysed as tone/ternary vowel length.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's morphological coding (Westermann 1912: accent on the stem syllable): where Gilley marks stress it is on the root syllable, never on affixes. It adds that in her analysis stress is grammatically contrastive (present vs absent on the root, signalling aspect/valency/iterativity) rather than an obligatory word-level prominence, and that Shilluk is tonal (3 levels). It does not give a placement rule of its own, and later work (Remijsen, Ayoker & Mills 2011; Remijsen et al. 2019, held by the project) reanalyses this 'stress' as tone/ternary vowel length - so it neither supports nor contradicts a positional statement; no contradiction with the catalog.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No positional word-stress rule is stated. 'Stress' in Shilluk is treated as a feature of the (monosyllabic) root syllable that is either present or absent in a given inflected verb form: its addition/absence, together with tone and root-vowel/consonant length, marks perfect vs imperfective aspect, readers vs benefactive role and iterativity; when present it sits on the root syllable (prefixes a-, prefixal transfixes and suffix -a are never described as stressed) and is written with a vertical/grave mark before the stressed syllable. Shilluk is described as having three level tones plus contours (sec. 2.3).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the stressed/unstressed contrast is paradigmatic (per verb form), not lexical exceptions. For Dinka (pp. 10-11) 'stress' is explicitly a cover term for extra-short vs short vowel length; for Shilluk p.5 links the phenomenon to Miller & Gilley 2001.
new_statements.identity_note: Gilley 2004 treats Shilluk (ISO shk) generally, mentioning work with 'two dialects of Shilluk' without naming them, alongside Dinka (Rek examples said representative of Rek, Bor, Agaar, Padang); only the Shilluk passages were used here. Gilley 1992/1988, Kohnen 1933 and Miller & Gilley 2001 were not opened, so nothing can be said about the variety they describe beyond 'Shilluk'.

(2) The classification set by morphology (stress on the monosyllabic stem, affixes unstressed) rests on a 1912 descriptive grammar; Westermann's companion Short Grammar (downloaded now, sec.10 p.8) independently restates it ('the stress does not lie on the vowel beginning or ending a word', i.e. affix vowels, 'most of the words are monosyllabic'). The modern specialist literature (Remijsen school 2011-2019, held/downloaded; Gilley 1992/2003, not obtainable online) treats Shilluk prosody as stem-syllable tone (7-9 categories) plus ternary vowel length, with affixes limited to level tones; the only modern 'stress' is Gilley's paradigmatic stem-syllable feature, which Remijsen, Ayoker & Jorgensen 2019 reject instrumentally. sources.quote: 'In addition to tone Gilley (1992, 2000 and 2003) distinguishes stressed words from unstressed words. Under her interpretation, stress is a distinctive feature at the syllable level which makes the whole unit to sound more prominent. Remijsen (personal communication), attributes what has been thought of as stress by Gilley to vowel length (V vs VV) and/or presence of a High Fall contour. My data supports Remijsen's analysis in this respect, and, thus I will not be discussing stress any further.' Confirms that Gilley 1992 posits a lexical/paradigmatic stress feature; no positional word-stress s
sources.locator: p. 9 (sec. 1.3) and the tone section ( lines 312, 1059-1065)
sources.note: Treats Shilluk nominal suprasegmentals as tone plus vowel length; mentions 'the placement of stress' only as one of Gilley's stem-internal number-marking devices (p. 9) and then explicitly sets stress aside (p. 27): Gilley's stressed-vs-unstressed words are reanalysed as vowel length and/or High Fall. Says nothing about stem-vs-affix prominence, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog's stem-stress (morphological) coding; it does show that the modern Edinburgh school does not operate with word stress at all.

sources.quote: Sets out the competing '2VL+Stress' hypothesis (Miller & Gilley 2001, 2007; Gilley 2003): binary vowel length plus a stress contrast on the stem syllable marking morphological (e.g. transitive vs antipassive) alternations, whose primary correlate is vowel shortening ('When a vowel is stressed, the syllable shortens to about half of its original length' Gilley 2003:104); argues on acoustic and morphological evidence that this stress feature is untenable and that the facts are three-level vowel length plus tone. The 'stress' at issue is paradigmatic on the stem syllable, not a word-position rule

sources.note: The only full-length phonology of Shilluk; per Reid 2009 and Remijsen et al. 2019 it posits a [stress] feature (stressed vs unstressed words/stem syllables). Our set by morphology coding rests solely on Westermann 1912; Gilley 1992 is the one unread work that could state (or deny) word-level stem-vs-affix prominence and would either upgrade the record to a modern phonology source or force a tonal/no-word-stress reclassify.

sources.quote: When a vowel is stressed, the syllable shortens to about half of its original length. Thus, a long stressed vowel will be about the same length as a short unstressed vowel. The short stressed vowel will become extra short. In this way, vowels in Shilluk and Dinka sound as though they exhibit three different vowel lengths. In [the following illustration] the different lengths and stress patterns are shown schematically. short stressed / short unstressed / long stressed / long unstressed [Gilley 2003:104, as quoted in Remijsen, Ayoker & Jorgensen 2019]
